# Conventions {#sec-conventions .unnumbered}

This page summarizes the visual and structural conventions
used throughout the book.

## Code

Two kinds of code appear. R code is shown in
syntax-highlighted blocks; its output is prefixed with `#>`
to make the boundary between input and output explicit:

```r
mean(c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5))
#> [1] 3
```

Shell commands, which recur constantly in this book, are
shown with a `$` prompt that is not part of the command:

```bash
$ zzc status
```

Inline code is in `monospace`. File and directory names
(`renv.lock`, `analysis/`) and command names (`make`, `zzc`)
are also set in monospace.

## The chapter card

Each numbered chapter opens with a card: an estimated
reading time, the chapters and the statistical knowledge it
assumes, three to five objectives phrased as questions the
reader should be able to answer by the end, and a short
outline of what follows. A reader who already knows the
material can check the objectives and skip ahead.

## Where a chapter sits on the stack

A computational result rests on nine layers, from the
hardware at the base to intrinsic non-determinism at the
top (@sec-levels works through all nine). Most chapters
open with a figure placing that chapter on the stack, with
the layers it **captures**, pins for the first time, drawn
in full color, and the layers it **validates**, checks
without itself pinning anything new, outlined. Every such
figure is a call to the same function, `plot_determinant_stack()`,
and its alt text is computed from the same call that draws
the figure, so the two cannot describe different layers.

## The folded Check

Most numbered sections end with a folded Check: a short
question testing comprehension of the section just read,
with the answer folded inside it so that attempting the
question is not optional. Expand the box to read the
question, attempt an answer, and only then expand the
Answer nested inside it.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: example

A short question testing comprehension of the just-read
material.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

The worked answer, with the reasoning that leads to it
rather than the conclusion alone.
:::
:::

## Callouts

Three kinds of callout appear, each with one job.

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## Verification

How to see that a claim actually holds, and, just as
important, how to make it fail on purpose. A gate that
cannot fail is not a gate.
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
## Pitfall

A specific way the preceding technique goes wrong in
practice, not a generic warning.
:::

::: {.callout-important}
## Restricted data

Where protected, identifiable, or data-use-agreement
restricted data may and may not go: which endpoints,
which tools, which repositories. This callout appears
wherever a technique could tempt a reader into committing,
depositing, or pasting such data.
:::

A fourth, smaller device, the honest level, closes most
chapters: one sentence naming the rung the chapter's own
practice reaches and what it still leaves exposed, not a
recital of the whole ladder.

::: {.callout-important}
## The honest level

One sentence, specific to this chapter, not the whole
ladder.
:::

## Habits

Seven numbered habits recur across the book, introduced in
full in @sec-intro and recalled in the closing chapter. A
rule of thumb in a chapter cites its habit by number, for
example 'habit 4', rather than restating it.

## The two datasets

The book works two datasets, and they have different jobs.
Which one a chapter uses is not arbitrary, so it is worth
setting out the division once.

**`survival::diabetic`** is real. It holds 394 records from
a randomized trial of laser photocoagulation for diabetic
retinopathy, with one row per eye and two eyes per patient.
It ships with every R installation, because `survival` is a
recommended package, so no chapter that uses it adds a
dependency the reader must install or the lockfile must
pin. It carries the computation: where the book fits a
model, draws a figure, or reports a number, that number
comes from real data and the reader can regenerate it.

**The incident-diabetes cohort is synthetic**, and is
written by `analysis/scripts/simulate_cohort.R` from a
fixed seed. It carries two threads the real data cannot.
The first is confidentiality: the extract holds record
numbers, names, and dates of birth, so the chapter on
version control can show a file that must never enter a
repository's history. No public dataset contains protected
information, by construction, so that lesson requires an
invented one. The second is data validation: the extract
carries deliberate defects, two date formats in one column,
a duplicated record, an implausible age, an inconsistently
coded sex, and missing outcomes, so that the tests in
@sec-testing have something to catch. Clean data would have
to be broken on purpose in any case.

The synthetic choice is not a compromise, and the book
would make it again with real data available. A committed
generator with a fixed seed is *more* reproducible than a
downloaded extract: it has no external dependency, no link
rot, and no access control, and a reader can regenerate it
byte for byte in a second. What it gives up is friction.
Invented messiness is tidier and stranger than the
messiness of an actual registry export, and a reader who
has only ever met generated data will be surprised by their
first real one.

The cohort compendium is still taking shape across the
book's chapters; not every chapter uses it yet, and a
reader who notices a chapter working from a different
example is seeing that in progress, not a different design.

## The one-quarter core path

The book is written for a one-quarter, ten-week course. The
table below marks a core path through it; a chapter marked
optional is not weaker material, only material a ten-week
schedule has no room for. An instructor with more time, or
a reader working alone, can take the whole book in order.

| Chapter | Status |
|---|---|
| Introduction | Core |
| The Reproducibility Crisis | Core |
| Levels of Reproducibility | Core |
| Version Control with Git and GitHub | Core |
| The Research Compendium | Core |
| Pinning Packages with renv | Core |
| Pinning the Environment with Docker | Core |
| Backends and Runtimes: Nix, Podman, and Apptainer | Optional |
| Literate Programming and the Rendered Report | Core |
| Automating the Analysis: Make and targets | Core for the Make section; `targets`, Snakemake, Nextflow, and workflowr are optional |
| Testing and Code Quality | Core |
| Continuous Integration and Verification | Core |
| Collaboration, Archiving, and Stewardship | Core |

## Cross-references

Sections, figures, and tables are referenced by their
Quarto label (`@sec-levels`, `@fig-ladder`, `@tbl-tools`).
Literature is cited by `@bibkey` and collected in the
References.
